ai-at-work.title: Trump Admin releases Anthropic  Mythos to be used by more than 100 US companies, agencies
ai-at-work.excerpt: Over 100 companies and government agencies are reportedly authorized to use Mythos 5, including their non-American employees.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The Trump administration has cleared Anthropic's Mythos 5 AI model for use across more than 100 US companies and government agencies, including access for non-US employees. This matters because it signals AI export controls are loosening and will reshape how organizations think about where their AI processing happens and who can access it. After years of watching enterprises tie themselves in compliance knots over data residency, somebody's about to learn the hard way that "authorized" and "actually compliant with your existing contracts" are two very different things.

ai-at-work.title: OpenAI limits GPT-5.6 rollout after government request, says restrictions shouldn’t be the norm
ai-at-work.excerpt: “We don’t believe this kind of government access process should become the long-term default,” says OpenAI. “It keeps the best tools from users, developers, enterprises, cyber defenders, and global pa
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI pumped the brakes on rolling out GPT-5.6 after a government request, though they're grumbling that this shouldn't become standard practice. Digital workplace leaders need to pay attention because AI deployment delays directly impact productivity plans, and we're entering murky territory around government influence on enterprise tools. Here's the thing though: OpenAI's complaint rings a bit hollow when they're simultaneously building closer ties with intelligence agencies, so workplace pros should probably stop assuming their favorite AI tool will be available when they need it.

ai-at-work.title: It’s not about Anthropic vs. OpenAI anymore
ai-at-work.excerpt: AI models have progressed to the point where their capabilities have real political consequences. Dealing with those consequences will require collective action.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The article argues we've moved past the early stage where individual AI companies matter more than the technology's actual impact on society and politics. This matters to digital workplace pros because the tools we're implementing in our organizations now have real consequences for how work gets done, who gets heard, and what information people see daily. Here's the thing: most companies are still picking between vendors like it's a taste test, when they should be asking harder questions about what these tools actually do to their culture and decision-making.

ai-at-work.title: OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip is Big Tech’s spiciest move away from Nvidia
ai-at-work.excerpt: Nvidia has dominated the AI chip market for years, but the era of total dependence might be ending. OpenAI just shared its plans to spice things up with Jalapeño, its custom inference chip built with
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI is developing a custom AI inference chip called Jalapeño with Broadcom to reduce reliance on Nvidia's dominance in the AI chip market. This matters to digital workplace pros because the tools powering your collaboration platforms, search, and generative AI features will increasingly run on diverse hardware, which could mean better performance, lower costs, and less supply chain fragility. Honestly, watching Big Tech finally break up with Nvidia feels like watching someone leave a bad relationship - it took longer than it should have, but at least it's happening.

tools-tech.title: US tells OpenAI to restrict access to its most powerful AI model
tools-tech.excerpt: US authorities are getting decidedly twitchy about frontier AI models. Just a couple of weeks after ordering Anthropic to prevent foreign companies from getting hold of its latest release, Mythos/Fabl
tools-tech.dwp_take: The Trump administration is pressuring OpenAI to delay releasing GPT-5.6 to the general public, citing national security concerns. This matters to digital workplace folks because enterprise AI tools are becoming strategically important, and government restrictions will reshape which AI capabilities actually make it to your organization's tech stack. After two decades watching tech adoption cycles, I can tell you that nothing kills innovation momentum quite like government telling companies to sit on their hands, so expect a lot of creative "workarounds" and whispered access deals in the months ahead.

tools-tech.title: AI agents are coming to China’s workplaces too
tools-tech.excerpt: Chinese tech giant Tencent is set to launch an AI assistant inside WeCom, its Slack-like collaboration tool for enterprises. The new tool, Dayuan, is built on the latest large language models from Chi
tools-tech.dwp_take: Tencent is launching Dayuan, an AI assistant within WeCom, its enterprise collaboration platform, powered by DeepSeek's latest language models. This matters because the global AI workplace race just got real competition from China, and digital workplace leaders can't ignore how quickly these tools are embedding themselves into the collaboration platforms people actually use every day. The irony is thick here: we're still figuring out what to do with our AI assistants while the market's already moving to the next version.

tools-tech.title: EU: Microsoft, Amazon cloud services could be classified as gatekeepers
tools-tech.excerpt: Following a seven-month investigation, the European Commission has reached a preliminary decision that Amazon’s and Microsoft’s cloud platforms — AWS and Azure, respectively — should be classified as
tools-tech.dwp_take: The European Commission concluded after months of investigating that AWS and Azure should be classified as gatekeepers under the EU's Digital Markets Act, which restricts the market dominance of tech giants. This matters because it could force Microsoft and Amazon to change how they operate their cloud platforms, affecting everything from pricing to data portability for the enterprise customers relying on them. Finally, someone's telling the big dogs to play fair, though I'd bet money both companies have already budgeted for the lawyers this will require.

tools-tech.title: Cyberattacks pose a ‘threat to life’ in Australia
tools-tech.excerpt: Australia’s Security Intelligence Organization (ASIO) has uncovered an attack on a critical infrastructure operator’s network. State-sponsored actors had compromised the network and were preparing to
tools-tech.dwp_take: Australia's spy agency discovered state-sponsored hackers had infiltrated a critical infrastructure operator's systems and were actively preparing sabotage operations. This matters to digital workplace pros because securing enterprise networks isn't just about protecting data anymore, it's about ensuring essential services don't go dark and potentially harm people. Turns out the scariest part of your job isn't defending against ransomware for financial data, it's that your workplace network might be connected to something that keeps hospitals running or power flowing.

digital-culture.title: Apple just closed its first unionized store. What does that mean for its workers?
digital-culture.excerpt: In 2022, an Apple Store outside of Baltimore became the first in the U.S. to unionize, fueled by worker frustrations over how they were treated during the pandemic. Two years later, they won a contrac
digital-culture.dwp_take: Apple closed its first unionized store in Baltimore after workers organized around pandemic-era treatment issues and won contract protections in 2022. This matters to digital workplace pros because it shows that even premium brands face real retention and culture problems when workers feel undervalued, and unionization becomes the outlet. Here's the thing: you can't Slack your way out of fundamental respect issues, and Apple just learned that the hard way.

digital-culture.title: JPMorgan fired an employee over a $642 deli platter. Now it owes him $4.25 million
digital-culture.excerpt: It took nearly two decades for Brent Ryan Bodner to build his career at JPMorgan. It took a deli platter to end it.In 2024, Bodner was fired from the bank after charging a $642.50 food order to his em
digital-culture.dwp_take: JPMorgan fired a longtime employee over a $642.50 catering charge he claimed was business-related while the bank insisted it was personal, and now they owe him $4.25 million in a legal settlement. This matters because it's a brutal reminder that inconsistent expense policies, poor documentation, and disproportionate disciplinary responses create legal liability that costs way more than the original dispute. The real lesson here isn't about the platter, it's that HR and finance teams need clear, consistently applied rules or they'll end up funding someone's retirement by accident.

digital-culture.title: Why menopause is employers’ $1.8 billion blind spot—and what leaders can do about it
digital-culture.excerpt: As companies work to build more inclusive, high-performing workplaces, one major workforce issue is still hiding in plain sight: menopause. Around 1 billion women globally are currently in perimenopau
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies are finally waking up to the fact that menopause affects productivity and retention, with an estimated 1.8 billion dollar impact on workplaces that ignore it. Digital workplace pros need to understand this because it directly affects how we design tools, policies, and support systems for a huge chunk of the workforce. After 30 years in this space, I'll say it straight: if your workplace strategy doesn't account for menopause, you're not actually building for inclusion, you're just performing it.

digital-culture.title: The Big Freeze: Why teams seize up under pressure (and how to avoid it)
digital-culture.excerpt: Across organizations, leaders are asking teams to move faster, adapt sooner, and make decisions with less certainty. Yet many are seeing the opposite: hesitation, silence, delayed decisions, and cauti
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company's arguing that when organizations demand speed without building the conditions for it, teams actually slow down and freeze up instead of accelerating. This matters because digital workplace leaders often inherit this mess and have to figure out why their fancy new collaboration tools aren't solving what's actually a culture and confidence problem. The irony is that slapping another app on people probably makes the Big Freeze worse, not better.

industry-news.title: Apple Overhauls Chip Roadmap, Ditches M6 Pro and Max for M7 Generation
industry-news.excerpt: Apple may skip the high-end M6 chips and shift premium Macs to AI-focused M7 processors, making the upgrade decision tougher for power users. The post Apple Overhauls Chip Roadmap, Ditches M6 Pro and
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple is jumping from M5 chips straight to M7 for its premium MacBook Pro and Mac Studio lines, skipping the M6 Pro and Max generation entirely. This matters because it means your enterprise Mac refresh cycles just got messier, and you'll have a longer window of older hardware circulating before the next generation lands. Honestly, this is fine for most office workers, but your creative teams are going to be very cranky about the wait, and your budget forecast just became someone else's problem.

industry-news.title: Hackers Claim French Employment Leak Exposes Over 1M Records, Health Data
industry-news.excerpt: Hackers claim 1M+ records tied to French employment apps were exposed, including HR files, health data, worker details, and plaintext passwords. The post Hackers Claim French Employment Leak Exposes O
industry-news.dwp_take: A hacker group claims to have stolen over a million records from French employment apps, including HR files, health data, and passwords stored in plaintext. This matters to digital workplace professionals because it's a brutal reminder that employee data security isn't optional and that basic practices like password hashing aren't suggestions. If your company is still storing passwords in plaintext in 2024, you deserve whatever happens next.

industry-news.title: New License Plate Reader Tech Could Track Phones, AirPods, and Smartwatches
